title: Clay bar and decontamination
audience: Car detailers preparing paint and glass for polishing or protection.
learningOutcomes: Test a washed panel by touch and identify embedded contamination before deciding to decontaminate.
Decontaminate in small, lubricated sections, and reshape or replace the clay as it loads.
Choose a fine-grade clay for most vehicles and explain why a medium grade needs polishing afterwards.

instruction.heading: What decontamination removes
instruction.body: Washing removes loose dirt but not everything. Embedded contamination includes tree sap, tar, brake dust, bird droppings and insects, and industrial fallout, which is embedded iron particles that leave a surface feeling rough after a wash. Some contamination lodges in the pores of the clear coat and cannot be seen, so touch is needed to find it. Decontamination does not remove swirls or scratches. A clay bar has no effect on those marks, so clay is preparation for polishing rather than a substitute for it. Iron removers react with iron deposits and can reduce the need for clay on some vehicles. Use an iron remover only as its label directs, and rinse it off fully before drying.

instruction.heading: Touch test and choosing the method
instruction.body: After a wash and dry, glide clean fingertips lightly over the paint in shade. A surface that does not feel smooth like polished glass has contamination. A clean plastic bag over the hand also makes rough spots easier to feel. Map the rough areas on the condition record, then choose the method. Iron remover suits iron deposits. Tar and sap often need the clay itself. Decontamination pads and towels, which have a urethane face, can be washed and reused and often replace clay for light contamination. A clay bar must be discarded once it has picked up heavy contamination or has been dropped on a dirty floor. Chemical decontaminants must not be used on a finish with a protective coating unless the coating's label allows it.

instruction.heading: Lubrication and technique
instruction.body: Clay works only on a lubricated surface. Without lubricant the clay sticks and drags, and marring follows. Use the clay maker's recommended lubricant, a quick detailer with cleaning power and little protection, or a diluted wash solution, following the label. Work in small sections, about 45 centimetres square, so the lubricant does not dry. Use straight, overlapping passes, horizontally or vertically, with light pressure, and let the clay absorb the contamination. The clay is finished when it glides without grabbing and makes no grinding sound. Wipe off the excess lubricant with a clean microfibre towel, using a fresh face for each section. Reshape the clay to expose clean material after each section, and break off a new piece if no fresh surface remains. A dropped piece is discarded. Avoid claying in direct sun, because the lubricant evaporates quickly.

instruction.heading: Grade, rewash and check
instruction.body: Use a fine-grade clay for most vehicles. A medium grade is more aggressive and usually leaves marring that needs polishing to remove. Fine grade cleans and leaves the surface ready. After the clay, rewash to remove loosened contamination and any clay residue, and dry by sheeting and blotting. Check the surface by touch again. A panel that still feels rough is decontaminated only as far as you have achieved, so record what remains and do not describe it as clean. The next step is polishing (“Polishing and paint correction: the difference”) or protection (“Paint protection choices: wax, sealant and coating”). Keep the clay and decontamination record with the condition map from “Vehicle condition and evidence”.

procedure: Wash and dry the vehicle in shade.
Touch-test each panel and map the rough areas on the condition record.
Apply iron remover where needed, following its label, and rinse it fully.
Mist lubricant onto a small section, about 45 centimetres square.
Glide the fine-grade clay with straight, overlapping passes and light pressure until it runs smoothly.
Wipe off the excess lubricant, and reshape the clay after each section.
Rewash, dry by sheeting and blotting, and recheck the surface by touch.

workedExamples.situation: A dark car has tree sap on the bonnet and brake dust on the lower panels. The paint feels gritty under the fingertips in shade.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which method for which area, and what is the limit?
workedExamples.reasoning: Apply iron remover to the lower panels as its label directs, rinse, then clay the lower panels with fine-grade clay in small sections. Test the sap on the bonnet with the clay on a small patch first. If the fine grade does not lift the sap, do not step up to a medium grade without a polishing plan and the owner's agreement. Record the areas still rough after the clay, and say so, rather than calling the paint clean.

workedExamples.situation: A clay bar is dropped on the garage floor while working on a silver car, and a colleague wants to continue with the same piece.
workedExamples.reasoning: Discard the piece. A dropped clay bar carries grit that will scratch the panel. Take a new piece, mist lubricant on the section, and continue. Note the drop in the job file, because the owner may ask about the delay.

equipmentAndPpe: Fine-grade clay, and a medium grade only for a planned job.
Clay lubricant, used as its label directs.
Clean microfibre towels, folded so each section gets a fresh face.
Iron remover and tar remover, each used as its label directs.
Decontamination pads or towels as an option, and a clay storage container.
PPE: gloves and eye protection for chemicals, as each SDS requires. Keep chemicals away from drains.

commonErrors.error: Claying dry or in direct sun.
commonErrors.prevention: Lubricate every section and work in shade.
Use light pressure and let the clay absorb the contamination.

commonErrors.error: Using a medium grade on a finish you need to keep.
commonErrors.prevention: Default to fine grade. A medium grade needs a polishing plan.

commonErrors.error: Describing clay as a way to remove swirls.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe clay as preparation. Swirls need polishing.
Rewash, dry and touch-check before polishing or protection.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Wash water and rinse water from decontamination carry removed material. Victorian EPA guidance says stormwater drains should carry only rainwater, and that commercial car washes that capture and treat wash water are the more responsible option.
Iron removers and tar removers are chemicals with labels and SDSs. Dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the label and SDS, not from this lesson.

qualityStandard: Each panel is touch-tested before and after clay, and the rough areas are recorded.
No dropped clay is used, and each section is lubricated before the clay touches it.
Panels are rewashed and dried, and the record states any contamination that remains.
documentationEvidence: Touch-test map added to the condition record.
Record of product, area, and the decision to step up or stop, with the rewash and recheck.
summary: Lubricate every section, use light pressure, and discard a dropped clay.
Default to fine grade, and rewash and recheck before polishing.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which best describes clay bar use?
options: It removes swirls and scratches from the paint in a single pass with no other steps
It replaces the wash, so the car does not need a separate shampoo step at all today
It removes embedded contamination from a lubricated surface and leaves it ready for polishing
It is best used dry, to save lubricant, and the bar can be kept dry during the work

knowledgeChecks.question: A clay bar is dropped on the floor. What is correct?
options: Discard it and use a new piece
Wipe it on a towel and carry on
Use it on the wheels only

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is fine grade usually preferred over medium grade for most vehicles?
options: Fine grade is faster, so it saves time on every job and is preferred by most detailers
A medium grade does not clean the paint at all, so it is only used for polishing work
A medium grade is more aggressive and usually leaves marring that needs polishing
Fine grade leaves the most marring, so it needs a second pass with a finer product
